summary: A blast wave drives the fireball outward; Taylor's scaling links its radius to the energy.

paragraphs.text: From here the picture is a side-on slice through the desert, and the view keeps widening. A blast wave pushes the hot air outward, so the fireball grows. Its bright outer edge is the shock front: air squeezed so hard that it glows.

The physicist G. I. Taylor worked out how such a blast grows. Radius depends on time to the power two-fifths, with the energy and the density of the air setting the scale: {{shock_law}}. At 25 ms it gives {{shock_r_25ms}}. He read the bright outer edge in published photographs as the shock front and estimated the yield from them.

At {{breakaway_time}} the front, {{breakaway_radius}} from the centre, grows too cool to glow and runs ahead of the fireball. Afterwards only a faint ring, where the air bends light, races across the desert, with a skirt of dust whipped up behind it.

The fireball itself keeps swelling more slowly: {{fireball_max_radius}}. Near the ground the wave reflects off the desert and merges with the first wave into a stronger front, called a Mach stem. Here it is drawn only as an illustration.

events.detail: At {{breakaway_time}} the shock front outruns the glowing fireball and begins to fade.
Once the shock front has cooled it no longer glows; only a faint ring remains.

callouts.text: Taylor read the bright outer edge in published photographs as the shock front, and from its growth estimated the yield.
The front outruns the fireball and cools below incandescence.
A faint ring where the air bends light races ahead, with dust behind it.
Near the ground the reflected wave merges with the first. Illustrative, not modelled.
The fireball is at its largest and cooling.
